title: 新一波单人AI游戏制作者赚钱了吗？并没有
content:
Are the new wave of solo AI game-makers making any money? No, not really – Mobilegamer.biz
Skip to content
Games made with AI tools like Claude Code are flooding the app stores – but very few of them appear to be generating any meaningful revenue or downloads.
As we’ve reported before, the new wave of AI coding and creation tools has led to
cloning getting even more aggressive
,
app review times slowing down
and even the
reverse-engineering of several top games to reveal their monetisation secrets
.
The mobilegamer.biz inbox has also been flooded with AI-written emails about AI-made games.
So we’ve been replying to most of them to ask: how many downloads did your game get, and have you made any money?
And the answers suggest that no, no-one is really making any money from their AI-made games. In some cases, hobbyists have spent thousands on Claude tokens to get their game made and have seen practically no return on that investment.
Some creators have used tools like Claude to jump on trends fast and generate some interest, but those success stories are few and far between. Over the summer, we reported on
38-0-0
, a football drafting game that managed to cut through and top the UK App Store charts.
38-0-0 creator Deniz Sancar didn’t want to reveal the game’s total earnings, but he told us that it has made enough money from ads and IAPs that he “could live off it full time” if he wasn’t also running his marketing firm Virlo. Downloads to date total around 300k on iOS and over 700k on Android. The game also monetises through its website and a Mac app.
We also covered the creation and launch of
Tennis Tycoon
, a management game made in Claude by a retired tennis pro. Its creator Iain Atkinson says total sales from the game come to around $3k, though the game cost him thousands in tokens to create.
“After
your article
came out my sales and downloads were about five times their normal daily rate,” Atkinson told us. “This game has always been less about the money for me though than it is about making something I’m passionate about and learning the process for building, releasing and managing app store games.”
Beyond that, it’s tough out there. Ahmed Alshuail released his Claude-made game
Sprout: Cozy Idle Garden
Google Play on August 30 and on the App Store on September 30. As of October 28, the game had generated 121 downloads and “about $6 in revenue, $4 from in-app purchases and roughly $2 from ads,” Alshuail told us.
Marc Fienberg created
Zen Ten Match
using a combination of Claude Code, Wikimedia Commons for images and Freesound for audio. He also used React Native and Supabase to power the backend, plus RevenueCat and AdMob for monetisation. The iOS edition of Zen Ten Match went live on September 22 with Android following on October 2, after two App Store reviews. As of October 13, Fienberg told us the game had 24 real players on iOS, 11 on Android and 39 in the browser – 74 players in total. Revenue from the first three weeks was “about $3, all from ads,” Fienberg told us.
Raúl Hernández Solano released
Hadadada: Fairy Game
on Google Play in early September. After around a month on sale, Solano told us the game had generated 31 installs by the end of the month, with seven active device installs as of October 7. “It has generated less than €0.10 in ad revenue so far, so effectively no meaningful income yet,” Solano told us.
Solo developer Yevhen Melnychenko told us that he worked on his roguelike deckbuilder
Goblin Card RPG: Tower Trials
for five months, using a combination of Claude Code, PixelLab and ElevenLabs. After about a month on the iOS App Store, it had generated 650 installs and around 70 on Android, where it launched several weeks later. Melnychenko says he’s likely to make about $50 per month from the game’s ads, and will also launch the title on Steam.
Maths puzzler
Calc Quest
was made by Arin Agrawal using Google’s Flutter platform, and has been live on iOS and Android since the start of the year. Agrawal claims his game has now reached over 25k players, but so far, the game has made around $120 through in-app purchases and ads, via AdMob.
Gökhan Us launched block puzzler
Fallmatch
in August, and told us that after a month on the market the game had generated 100 downloads between iOS and Android. He later told us he’d spent about $500 on a Google App campaign to get installs moving, and later saw about 1,600 installs through Google Play, but would not share revenue figures.
William-Arno Clément released gay mermaid RTS
Ego Fabula
in early September, and told us his game was downloaded once in its first week; Ivan Soyer told us he spent $1500 on AI tools and tokens to make
Dusk Climber
, which has been on the app stores for a month and has generated 1,000 downloads and no revenue at all, yet.
Another solo game-maker Ben Henderson told us that his pet project
HotShot: Fireball Pool
has been on Google Play since 26 October and the App Store since 30 October and has made £0: “No in-app purchases yet, and iOS downloads are in single figures a week.”
Solo developer Keith Jacobs says he has taken both approaches. In the past he has spent about $25k hiring contractors to make his first app,
Queztions
. More recently, he used Claude to make another game,
Endless Racing: Dingo Dasher
, in less than two weeks at practically no cost.
“I have not yet made any significant amounts of money from my games, but the reasons for that are more complicated than whether I used AI or not,” he told us. “Queztions has been done without using AI in any significant way, and Dingo Dasher was made almost exclusively with AI, and neither is outperforming the other in terms of revenue generation.”
“I see AI as a great equaliser in the playing field,” added Jacobs. “I don’t have massive budgets or a huge team of people with fifty years of programming experience to call on, but I feel I can still put out products that represent my vision and ethos in a very demanding industry.”
